first_impression.reaction: Okay, this isn't the usual 'say I do in paradise' fluff. The intro tells us it's a sequence over weeks, not one afternoon, which is exactly the kind of thing we'd need to know if Java or Bali stays on the list. I skimmed the key takeaways and the legal one made me stop and actually read. The title is a bit clickbait-y though ('You Did Not Know?').

journey.quote: A Javanese wedding is not one ceremony. It is a sequence that can begin months before the day, with a first meeting between families, and close with a son or daughter kneeling before their parents.
journey.reaction: Good opener. Calm, specific, no fairytale language. It earned the skim.

journey.quote: Siraman, the cleansing bath, and midodareni, a quiet night of advice and prayer, both fall before the vow, so elders need to arrive early.
journey.reaction: This is the bit that matters to us. If half our guests are flying in, and grandparents need to be there days early, that changes flights and accommodation. Practical, not just pretty.

journey.quote: For a destination wedding, plan two private bathing spaces and a gap in the run sheet so elders can move between them.
journey.reaction: That's an insider detail. Nobody thinks about two private spaces at a villa until it's too late. This is the kind of line that makes me think they've actually run one of these.

journey.quote: At a hired villa or hotel, agree early where the janur and plants will go and who installs them.
journey.reaction: Useful, and an honest trade-off. Though it does make me wonder: is that something the Wedded Advisor sorts with the venue, or are we the ones chasing it?

journey.quote: It is a quiet family evening, not a hen's or buck's night. Keep guest entertainment for another night, and warn the families before booking an early call the next morning.
journey.reaction: Love this. Exactly the sort of clash that would cause friction between our friends and the older relatives. Honest and practical.

journey.quote: It is often told that the groom steps on the egg, a step many families call ngidak endog or wiji dadi.
journey.reaction: I get that they're being careful, but 'it is often told' shows up so many times it starts to read like a footnoted essay. Combined with all the 'a 2022 study in Jurnal...' lines, it's heavy going when I'm skimming on my phone. I'd forward the legal section to my parents, not the middle.

journey.quote: We have not found an official source that sets out those differences.
journey.reaction: Weirdly, this makes me trust them more. They're not pretending to know. But a photo or a real wedding would answer what this paragraph can't.

journey.section: Can Australians legally marry in Java or Bali?
journey.quote: Under Indonesian Law No. 1 of 1974, both partners must hold the same religion, or one must convert.
journey.reaction: This is the line that would actually change our decision. Glad it's stated plainly instead of buried. Confidence the legal side is sorted is one of our big things, and this section is clear and well sourced.

journey.section: Can Australians legally marry in Java or Bali?
journey.quote: Civil Registry Offices do not normally accept a CNI issued more than 3 months before.
journey.reaction: Specific timing detail. This is the sort of thing I'd want someone else to track for us so we're not on spreadsheets for 18 months.

journey.section: Can Australians legally marry in Java or Bali?
journey.quote: Smartraveller also notes that the revised criminal code includes penalties for cohabitation and sex outside marriage.
journey.reaction: Hang on. We're not married yet and we'd be sharing a room on the pre-wedding trip. This is dropped in with no follow-up about what it means for couples or guests in practice. It's honest, but it leaves me a bit uneasy.

journey.section: Planning a Javanese wedding with both families
journey.quote: A Wedded Advisor is your single point of contact for everything around them, with the fee and inclusions agreed in writing before you commit.
journey.reaction: Fee and inclusions in writing up front speaks straight to our hidden-costs worry. 'Single point of contact' is better than 'end-to-end', but I still don't know what 'everything around them' actually covers: guest transfers? the juru paes? the KUA paperwork?

unanswered_questions: Does the Wedded Advisor actually handle the legal paperwork timing (CNI, notice of intention, KUA), or just point us to the embassy?
Who gets our grandparents and international guests from the airport to the venue in Java, and how far are typical venues from Yogyakarta or Solo airports?
Do you work with your own juru paes, gamelan musicians and elders who lead the rites, or are they found per wedding?
Is there a real Javanese or Indonesian wedding you've planned, with venue and date, that we can look at?
What does the cohabitation law mean in practice for an unmarried couple and guests staying at a villa or hotel?
Is Java or Bali the more realistic base for a 60 to 90 guest wedding with half flying in?

turn_offs_found.quote: What Are the Javanese Wedding Traditions You Did Not Know?
turn_offs_found.why: The headline reads a little like listicle clickbait. The body is far more grown-up than the title suggests.

would_share_with: Partner (the legal section and key takeaways)
Parents, since they're contributing and would want to understand the family-led steps and the arrive-early timing

cta_reaction.quote: If you are weighing Java, Bali or a wedding at home, [Wedded Concierge](/wonderland-concierge) is a good place to begin that conversation.
cta_reaction.why: It's soft, not hard-sell, which I like. I'd click through to see what Concierge is, but I wouldn't enquire off this post alone. We'd want a couple more posts and one real wedding first, and ideally a clear picture of what the Advisor handles versus what we handle.

top_3_changes: Add a short 'what we handle for you' line or box near the end: guest arrivals and transfers for elders arriving early, booking the juru paes and musicians, and keeping the CNI and registry timing on track. Right now 'everything around them' is vague.
Follow the cohabitation sentence with one practical line on what it means for unmarried couples and guests, or a pointer to where to check, so it informs rather than alarms.

Cut back the repeated 'it is often told' and inline journal names in the tradition sections so it skims easily on a phone, and link one real Javanese or Indonesian wedding (venue and date) if one exists.
